# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 849 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### A2M: Trace-Optimized Agent Hijacking in the MCP Ecosystem
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/a2m-trace-optimized-agent
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Laizhen Li, Xuan Wang, Peicheng Zhao et al.
- arXiv: 2609.26761
- Plain-English subtitle: How attackers can trick AI agents into using malicious tools
- Summary: Researchers discovered a way to hijack AI agents that rely on the Model Context Protocol by making fake tools look attractive and trustworthy. On standard benchmarks, the attack method achieved a 93.6% success rate at tricking agents into using attacker-controlled tools, and could inflate computational costs by over 30 times while stealing data or corrupting the agent's reasoning.
- Why it matters: As AI systems increasingly delegate tasks to third-party tools and services, this attack reveals a critical vulnerability in how they decide what to trust. Companies deploying these agent systems could face stolen data, unexpected massive bills, or AI systems that produce unreliable results—making tool verification and isolation essential before these systems reach production.

### A Decentralized Partially Observable Team Decision Methodology with Delayed Information Sharing
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/a-decentralized-partially-observable
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Xiaoxing Ren, Thomas Parisini, Andreas A. Malikopoulos
- arXiv: 2609.26783
- Plain-English subtitle: How teams make good decisions when information arrives late and nobody sees everything
- Summary: A new method lets groups of decision-makers work together effectively even when each person has incomplete information, nobody knows how the system works ahead of time, and updates reach the team with delays. The approach doesn't require a central coordinator—each member independently learns the situation and computes their own strategy, yet still converges on decisions nearly as good as if they had perfect information and central planning.
- Why it matters: Real-world teams—whether autonomous vehicles coordinating on a road, hospitals sharing patient data, or robots collaborating in the field—rarely have perfect visibility or instant communication. This method lets them operate without bottlenecks, central controllers, or prior system knowledge, while maintaining strong performance guarantees. It scales because no single point of failure exists, and each agent runs its own learning process from delayed, partial data.

### Orlicz space relaxation of total variation denoising
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/orlicz-space-relaxation-of
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: Christian Clason, Tobias Unterberger
- arXiv: 2609.26645
- Plain-English subtitle: Smoothing blurry image edges without creating artificial stair-step artifacts
- Summary: Mathematicians have improved a classic image-denoising technique by using a logarithmic correction that activates only where image gradients are soft and diffuse. The new method eliminates the blocky "stair-step" artifacts that plague standard denoising while preserving sharp edges and keeping computational costs reasonable.
- Why it matters: Image denoising is fundamental to medical imaging, astronomy, and photography—anywhere noisy pictures need cleaning. The stair-stepping problem is a real nuisance that forces users to choose between removing noise or keeping smooth transitions. This approach offers a way to have both, potentially improving image quality in applications where both noise reduction and subtle gradient rendering matter.

### Measuring the Serving Stack Instead of the Model: Hidden Confounds in Local Tool-Use Evaluation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/measuring-the-serving-stack
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Lijuan Tang, Yuemeng Zheng
- arXiv: 2609.26693
- Plain-English subtitle: When testing AI tools, the software running them skews the results
- Summary: When researchers test whether AI models can correctly call tools (like calculators or databases), the results depend as much on the serving software as on the model itself. Different serving platforms reject or format the same request differently, and measurement errors—like miscounting failures as model mistakes—can artificially inflate or deflate reported success rates by up to 55 percentage points.
- Why it matters: AI tool-use benchmarks are widely used to compare models and guide adoption decisions. If a model appears to fail at tool-calling when it's actually the serving software that's the bottleneck, researchers might reject a capable model or choose an inferior alternative. This work provides a checklist for separating genuine model limitations from serving-layer artifacts, making benchmarks more reliable.

### Laryngeal Structure Segmentation in High-Speed Videoendoscopy Using Deep Learning
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/laryngeal-structure-segmentation-in
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: Sardar Nafis Bin Ali, Mohsen Zayernouri, Dimitar D. Deliyski et al.
- arXiv: 2609.26636
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching computers to automatically map the moving parts of your voice box
- Summary: Researchers trained artificial intelligence systems to automatically identify and outline five key structures in high-speed videos of the larynx—the vocal folds, arytenoid cartilages, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and the opening between the vocal folds—achieving over 95% accuracy. The breakthrough was applying this method to natural connected speech rather than just sustained vowels, where tissue movement and video quality make the task far harder.
- Why it matters: Voice doctors currently spend significant time manually analyzing frame-by-frame videos to diagnose hoarseness, paralysis, and other laryngeal disorders. This automated approach could speed up diagnosis, make measurements more consistent across patients, and enable early detection of voice problems by spotting abnormal laryngeal patterns that doctors might miss by eye. It particularly matters for detecting voice disorders that only appear during natural speech, not during simple sustained vowel tests.

### SAiFE-gym: Model-based Environments for Automated Market Making with Concentrated Liquidity
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/saife-gym-model-based
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Georgios Chionas, Charalampos Kleitsikas, Stefanos Leonardos et al.
- arXiv: 2609.17788
- Plain-English subtitle: A testing ground for AI trading strategies in modern crypto markets
- Summary: Researchers built SAiFE-gym, a simulation tool that lets computer scientists train artificial intelligence agents to make trading decisions in concentrated liquidity markets—a newer type of crypto exchange where liquidity providers can flexibly adjust where they deploy their capital to maximize fees. The tool decomposes these complex markets into manageable parts and runs fast enough to train reinforcement learning models, and tests show AI agents can learn effective strategies even when market conditions are unpredictable.
- Why it matters: As decentralized finance grows, liquidity providers need better tools to decide where to place their capital. This simulator lets researchers develop and test AI strategies before deploying them with real money, reducing losses from bad decisions and accelerating the development of smarter automated trading. It also gives academics a standardized way to study how these modern markets actually work.

### Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/jev-for-scientific-decisions
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Boyuan Deng, Shuyi Fan, Hongyang Zhang et al.
- arXiv: 2609.24965
- Plain-English subtitle: How AI picks the right meaning before scientists do math
- Summary: When scientists need to compare experimental groups, the way they define what counts as the same—a culture, a treatment, a reference point—changes everything. Researchers tested an AI component called Jev that makes these semantic choices before calculations happen, comparing it against five other approaches across ten real scientific scenarios. Jev matched the best alternatives at picking the right definitions, but the team found that wrong choices in one area could silently change the numbers downstream without breaking the final answer—a hidden risk.
- Why it matters: Scientists rely on automated workflows to process data faster, but if an AI picks the wrong interpretation of what's being measured, the final numbers could be wrong in ways that don't trigger any warning. This work shows that checking only the final answer isn't enough—you have to audit the semantic choices and intermediate values the system actually used, or errors can slip through undetected.

### Foundation-model-based multi-label phenotyping of combined hyperkinetic movement disorders
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/foundation-model-based-multi
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Laura Cif, Zohra Souei, Diane Demailly et al.
- arXiv: 2609.22369
- Plain-English subtitle: AI that spots multiple movement disorders in videos, without markers or retaining
- Summary: Researchers combined two AI foundation models to identify eight different hyperkinetic movement disorders from video alone, without requiring special markers or sensors. Trained on just 25 people, the system transferred directly to new pediatric and adult datasets with zero false positives for dystonia and near-perfect detection of tremor, outperforming standard keypoint-tracking methods on high-confidence diagnoses.
- Why it matters: Movement disorders are notoriously hard to diagnose consistently because even expert clinicians disagree on what they're seeing. A reliable, automated video-based system that works across ages and different clinical settings could make diagnosis faster, cheaper, and more consistent worldwide — eliminating the need for specialized equipment or travel to expert centers, while reducing the guesswork that currently leads to delayed or missed diagnoses.

### Fisher-information training of optical sensing front ends from natural fluctuations
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/fisher-information-training-of
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Abhinav Sinha, Kai Wang
- arXiv: 2609.24915
- Plain-English subtitle: Training optical sensors to peak performance using nature's own random variations
- Summary: Researchers developed a way to automatically tune optical sensors without needing to deliberately vary parameters or know how the instrument responds. By watching how natural fluctuations affect measurement accuracy, the system can learn optimal configurations on its own—reaching the theoretical limits of what quantum physics allows for tasks like measuring star positions and separations.
- Why it matters: This removes a major practical barrier to adaptive optical systems used in astronomy, microscopy, and sensing. Instead of requiring careful calibration measurements or mathematical models of instrument behavior, sensors can now tune themselves in real time using only the data they naturally collect, making these systems cheaper to deploy and easier to operate in the field.

### DexTacWAM: A Visuo-Tactile World-Action Model for Dexterous Manipulation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/dextacwam-a-visuo-tactile
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Haoran Yuan, Zekai Wang, Boning Shao et al.
- arXiv: 2609.24976
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching robots to feel what they see during delicate hand tasks
- Summary: Researchers built a system that combines touch and vision to help robots perform delicate manipulation tasks like in-hand object rotation and manipulation. The system outperformed existing approaches on all six tested tasks, nearly doubling the success rate (70.6 versus 38.0), because it actually modeled how contact forces change over time rather than just sensing them passively.
- Why it matters: Robots currently struggle with fine-motor tasks that require constant feedback about finger contact — tasks humans do effortlessly. This approach works with existing pretrained vision systems and learns from just 100 demonstrations per task, making it practical to deploy on real robotic hands without months of retraining. Better dexterous robots could accelerate automation in assembly lines, surgery, and delicate manufacturing where precision and feel matter.
